This article shows four tools for time-to-event reports: a proportional-hazards audit,
cumulative incidence with competing events, a Fine-Gray regression, and pooling over multiple
imputations. All data are simulated.

## 1. Is the proportional hazards assumption reasonable?

`tbl_schoenfeld_audit()` runs the Schoenfeld-residual test (`survival::cox.zph()`) for each term and
for the model as a whole, and flags terms below `alpha`.

```{r schoenfeld}
fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = lung)
tbl_schoenfeld_audit(fit)
```

A small p-value is a prompt to look at the scaled residuals (`plot(cox.zph(fit))`), not proof of a
problem: with many events a trivial departure is flagged. Typical remedies are a time-varying
coefficient, stratification on the term, or a restricted mean survival analysis. A tidymodels
`workflow` or parsnip `model_fit` that wraps a `coxph` engine is accepted as well.

## 2. Competing risks: cumulative incidence

When a patient can have more than one kind of event (progression or death without progression),
`1 - Kaplan-Meier` with the other cause censored overstates the incidence of each. The Aalen-Johansen
estimate does not.

```{r cif-data}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 400
d <- data.frame(
  id = seq_len(n),
  arm = rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = n / 2),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 62, 9))
)
rate1 <- 0.06 * ifelse(d$arm == "Treatment", 0.6, 1) * exp(0.02 * (d$age - 62))
rate2 <- 0.04
t1 <- rexp(n, rate1)
t2 <- rexp(n, rate2)
cens <- runif(n, 5, 30)
d$time <- pmin(t1, t2, cens)
d$type <- ifelse(d$time == cens, 0L, ifelse(d$time == t1, 1L, 2L))
table(d$type, d$arm)
```

```{r cif-table}
cif <- tbl_cumulative_incidence(d, "time", "type", group_col = "arm", times = c(5, 10, 20))
cif
```

```{r cif-plot}
plot_cumulative_incidence(cif, facet = TRUE)
```

Code `1` is the cause of interest and `2` the competing event; `0` is censoring. The table and plot
are descriptive: they do not test or adjust for anything.

## 3. Competing risks: Fine-Gray regression

`tbl_fine_gray_single()` fits the subdistribution hazard model of one cause for one predictor at a
time (it uses `cmprsk::crr()`).

```{r fine-gray, eval = requireNamespace("cmprsk", quietly = TRUE)}
rbind(
  tbl_fine_gray_single(d, "time", "type", "arm"),
  tbl_fine_gray_single(d, "time", "type", "age")
)
```

The estimate is a **subdistribution hazard ratio**: it speaks about the cumulative incidence of the
cause of interest. It is not the hazard ratio of a Cox model that censors the competing event, and
the two answer different questions. Report the one that matches the question (the incidence a
patient faces, or the rate among those still at risk), and say which.

## 4. Pooling multiple imputations

Fit the same model to each of `m` imputed data sets, collect the tidy results, and pool with
Rubin's rules. Here the imputations are simulated draws of a covariate with missing values.

```{r impute}
set.seed(7)
lung2 <- na.omit(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex")])
lung2$ph.ecog <- lung$ph.ecog[as.integer(rownames(lung2))]
miss <- is.na(lung2$ph.ecog)
m <- 10
fits <- lapply(seq_len(m), function(i) {
  x <- lung2
  x$ph.ecog[is.na(x$ph.ecog)] <- sample(na.omit(lung2$ph.ecog), sum(miss), replace = TRUE)
  coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = x)
})
tidy_fits <- lapply(fits, function(f) {
  s <- summary(f)$coefficients
  data.frame(term = rownames(s), estimate = s[, "coef"], std.error = s[, "se(coef)"])
})
```

`pool_imputations()` pools each term. Pool on the log hazard ratio scale and use `exponentiate = TRUE`
to report hazard ratios.

```{r pool}
pool_imputations(tidy_fits, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

With few observations the large-sample degrees of freedom are too optimistic. Give the complete-data
degrees of freedom (for example `N - k`) as `df_complete` to get the Barnard-Rubin small-sample
adjustment:

```{r pool-br}
n_obs <- nrow(lung2)
pool_imputations(tidy_fits, df_complete = n_obs - 3)[, c("term", "df", "p.value", "fmi")]
```

A term that is missing from any imputation is an error, not a silent drop.

### Model-level fit

`glance_imputations()` pools the one-row summaries (`broom::glance()` output) in the same way: the mean over
the imputations with its spread, and, where the glance has a `std.error.<statistic>` column (such as the
concordance), a Rubin standard error and interval.

```{r glance}
glances <- lapply(fits, function(f) {
  s <- summary(f)
  data.frame(concordance = unname(s$concordance[1]),
             std.error.concordance = unname(s$concordance[2]),
             logLik = f$loglik[2])
})
glance_imputations(glances)
```

The pooled concordance is the mean of C-indices from separately completed data sets, not the C-index of
a pooled model.
